content.title: About
content.content: Brazil nuts are the edible seeds of the Brazil nut tree (Bertholletia excelsa), native to the tropical rainforests of the Amazon basin. The nuts have a creamy, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. They are eaten raw, roasted, or salted, and are used in baking, desserts, spreads, and nut milks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brazil nuts are among the largest nuts in the world, weighing 5–10 g each.
They are extremely rich in selenium: one nut can meet an adult's daily requirement.
The Brazil nut tree can live over 1,500 years and only fruits intermittently.
Wild animals such as toucans and monkeys traditionally drop the nuts to the ground for collection.
Brazil nuts are sometimes called “paradise nuts” because of their high content of healthy fats.

items.title: High in selenium
items.content: Selenium is a potent antioxidant that supports the immune system and thyroid function.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Most of the fat is monounsaturated and polyunsaturated, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids muscle and nerve function and supports energy metabolism.

items.title: Rich in protein and fiber
items.content: Helps promote satiety and supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine and folate contribute to carbohydrate metabolism and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: Brazil nuts can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Excess selenium intake
items.content: Consuming too many can lead to selenosis, a condition caused by selenium toxicity.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: They are energy‑dense, so portion control is recommended.

items.title: Digestive difficulty
items.content: Large nuts may be hard to digest for people with gastrointestinal issues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brazil nuts can be enjoyed as a snack, added to granola, yogurt, salads, baked goods, or made into nut butter. They are often roasted with a pinch of salt to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store nuts in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent fat oxidation. Discard nuts that smell rancid.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is the meat of the domestic bird (Gallus gallus domesticus). It has a mild flavor, tender texture, and is one of the most widely consumed protein sources worldwide. Chicken can be prepared by boiling, frying, baking, stewing, or adding to salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed by humans.
More than 130 million tonnes of chicken meat are produced globally each year.
Chicken breast is the leanest cut, while thighs are juicier and more flavorful.
Bones and skin are often used to make stocks and sauces.
Chicken readily absorbs herbs, spices, and marinades, making it extremely versatile.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken contains about 31 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skin‑less breast meat is very low in saturated fat, suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which aid metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bones, immunity and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Selenium and vitamin B6 help maintain a healthy immune response.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may contain Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed chicken products (deli meats, nuggets) often contain high levels of salt.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: Ready‑to‑eat chicken dishes can include flavor enhancers and additives that may not suit everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken can be baked, pan‑fried, boiled, steamed, or stewed with vegetables. For vegetable‑based dishes, bite‑size pieces of breast or thigh are often sautéed and then simmered with carrots, broccoli, peppers, and other veggies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh chicken should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen chicken retains quality for up to 9 months at –18 °C. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or a grayish color, which indicate spoilage.

green-peas-ns-as-to-form-cooked.title: Green peas, NS as to form, cooked

content.title: About
content.content: Green peas (Pisum sativum) are edible seeds harvested while still immature. The NS (non‑sprouted) form, when cooked, retains a vivid green color, a tender texture, and a mildly sweet flavor. Peas are commonly used in soups, purees, salads, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas are one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for more than 5,000 years.
A 100 g serving of cooked peas provides about 5 g of high‑quality plant protein.
Being a legume, peas fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil.
Cooking preserves most of the B‑vitamins and vitamin C present in fresh peas.
Peas are increasingly used to make plant‑based milks and protein powders.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Pea protein contains all essential amino acids, making it a valuable plant‑based protein source.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestive health, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B6, and folate in peas aid energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Peas provide iron, magnesium, phosphorus, and potassium, important for blood formation, muscle function, and electrolyte balance.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Peas raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes or diabetes.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas, ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Gas‑producing oligosaccharides
items.content: Peas contain oligosaccharides that can cause bloating and flatulence in sensitive people.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Large amounts of peas may increase uric acid levels, which can be problematic for gout sufferers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked green peas can be enjoyed as a standalone side, tossed into salads, added to soups, stews, or pureed for dips. They also pair well with rice, quinoa, or grain bowls to boost protein content.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked peas in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. For longer keeping, freeze portions in freezer‑safe bags; they retain quality for up to 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Melba toast is a thin, crisp cracker made from toasted bread without the crust. It was originally created in the early 20th century in Australia and named after opera singer Melba Johnson. The toast is usually sold as small square or rectangular pieces that break easily and are perfect for topping with a variety of spreads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first Melba toast recipe appeared in cookbooks of the 1920s.
They are popular in diet plans because they are low‑calorie and contain no added sugar.
In the United States Melba toast is often served with pâté, cream cheese, or avocado as an appetizer.
Their delicate texture makes them ideal for creating crostini in fine‑dining restaurants.
In some countries they are referred to as “crackers” or “biscottes” depending on local terminology.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One piece of Melba toast contains about 10–12 kcal, making it a convenient snack for weight control.

items.title: Rich in complex carbohydrates
items.content: The toast provides slowly digestible carbs that help maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: These crackers contain fiber that supports normal digestion.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Melba toast contains virtually no fat, suitable for low‑fat diet regimes.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Small amounts of thiamine and niacin contribute to energy metabolism.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Made from wheat bread, they can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties are salted; individuals monitoring sodium intake should choose unsalted versions.

items.title: Brittle texture
items.content: The thin pieces can break into sharp shards, posing a choking hazard for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Melba toast is served as a base for pâtés, cream cheese, caviar, avocado, smoked salmon, or vegetable dips. It can also be added to salads for crunch or enjoyed plain as a light snack with nut butter.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep Melba toast in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crispness.

nachos-beef-or-pork-with-beans.title: Nachos with Beef or Pork and Beans

content.title: About
content.content: Nachos are crispy corn chips topped with a flavorful blend of beef or pork, beans, cheese, and spices. The dish is popular in Mexican and American cuisines as a snack or a light meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional nachos are made from corn tortillas that are fried or baked until golden.
The meat‑and‑bean combination traces back to Tex‑Mex cooking, where beans were a cheap source of protein.
The melted cheese is often a mix of cheddar and processed Mexican cheese, giving a characteristic stretchy texture.
Nachos gained mainstream popularity in the 1970s in the United States through restaurant chains that served them with salsa and guacamole.
There is a vegetarian version using beans and vegetables, but the classic recipe includes meat.

items.title: Protein from meat
items.content: Beef and pork provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Fiber from beans
items.content: Beans are rich in soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both meat and beans contain B6 and B12 vitamins, important for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish supplies iron, zinc, and magnesium, which aid immune function and metabolic processes.

items.title: Antioxidants in spices
items.content: Paprika, cumin, and chili contain antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese and ready‑made sauces often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Beef, pork, and cheese add saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑related conditions.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Spicy ingredients
items.content: Chili and other hot spices can irritate the stomach of sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve nachos hot, sprinkled with shredded cheese that melts from the heat. Add sautéed beef or pork cooked with onion and spices, and drained beans. Accompany with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, or a squeeze of lime.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep plain chips in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 2 weeks. Store the cooked meat mixture and beans in the refrigerator for no more than 3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave before serving to restore crispness.

pork-potatoes-and-vegetables-including-c.title: Pork with Potatoes and Vegetables in Tomato Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish combines tender pork, boiled or roasted potatoes, carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale) in a flavorful tomato‑based sauce. It provides protein, complex carbohydrates and a wide range of vitamins, making it suitable for family meals or athletic nutrition.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomatoes used in the sauce are rich in lycopene, a potent antioxidant that becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
Pork is a good source of vitamin B12, essential for blood formation and nervous system function.
Broccoli contains sulforaphane, a compound studied for its potential anti‑cancer properties.
Potatoes retain most of their potassium when cooked with the skin on.
Dark‑green leafy greens such as spinach are high in iron and folate, supporting healthy blood.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Pork supplies all essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: The meal provides thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Potato (especially with skin), carrots and leafy greens add soluble and insoluble fiber for digestive health.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and carotenoids from carrots help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Vitamin C from tomatoes and broccoli boosts the immune response.

items.title: Processed meat concerns
items.content: Frequent consumption of heavily fried or processed pork may increase cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce often contains added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Vegetable allergies
items.content: Rarely, individuals may be allergic to broccoli or leafy greens.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Pork must be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C to eliminate salmonella and trichinella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, optionally alongside whole‑grain sides or a fresh salad. Leftovers store well in the fridge and can be reheated in a microwave or skillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before consuming.
